Streamflow forecasting in SAGE

Jasper A. Vrugt · November 26, 2026

How will a watershed respond to the rain expected over the next few days? The new Forecast tab in SAGE brings that question into the same program we use to train and evaluate hydrologic models. It takes a trained model, uses recent weather to bring the watershed to its starting conditions, and uses forecast weather to simulate streamflow over the days ahead.

View the full Forecast tab

From recent weather to forecast discharge

A forecast starts before the first day on the map. During spin-up, the model uses recent meteorological inputs to initialize its estimates of watershed storage. Those states carry the effects of earlier weather into the forecast. The same incoming storm can produce very different hydrographs in a dry basin and in one that is already wet.

See where flows change, then look at when

The Forecast tab offers two views of the same forecast. The maps let you scan across basins and compare discharge from one lead day to the next on a common color scale. The flow-category view puts the predicted discharge in the context of each basin’s own thresholds, so a modest discharge in a small stream can stand out when it is high for that basin.

The time-series panel gives you a closer look at an individual basin. Rainfall bars show when the model receives precipitation. The hydrograph below shows how discharge responds through spin-up and into the forecast period. The expanded forecast view makes it easier to see the timing of the rise, the peak, and the subsequent recession.

A Thanksgiving storm in the five-day forecast

New York City moved the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, November 28, as a coastal storm was expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding. In the SAGE forecast for the same period, several basins in the broader New York region reach the high or extreme high streamflow classes. These colors show how forecast river discharge compares with each basin's own flow thresholds. The city's advisory covers wind and coastal flooding as well.

New York City Emergency Management advisory

A common benchmark for conceptual models

Based on Xilan’s rainfall–runoff comparison, we’re adding a regionally trained long short-term memory (LSTM) benchmark to SAGE. It will use the same training, evaluation, and testing periods as the conceptual rainfall–runoff (CRR) models. The GUI will display the LSTM and CRR results alongside each other so users can compare performance over identical periods.

Other modules and capabilities are being developed as we speak. For example, we’ve implemented a GPU version of SAGE and are running a few more tests before making it available. We plan to include it in the next release.

Meet Olivier

Meet Olivier, my mini goldendoodle and SAGE’s in-app guide. He gives tips about the view you’re using. In the Attribution view, for example, he explains how to read the contributions of hydrologic model parameters to the loss gradient. Olivier is still in training. In a future release, we plan to let you ask him questions about SAGE, its settings, and what the options do.
